Fallacious

/fuh-LAY-shuhs/ - the stress falls on LAY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fallacious means based on unsound or misleading reasoning.

His proof that the team wins whenever he wears the lucky socks is fallacious—the team also wins plenty of games while the socks stay home.

Worked Example

The debate coach circled the closing argument in red: 'Every great inventor was laughed at; people laugh at me; therefore I am a great inventor.' The reasoning is fallacious—being laughed at is shared by geniuses and crackpots alike, so it proves membership in neither group.

Fallacious is not the same as 'false': the speaker might even turn out to be a great inventor. The word condemns the argument, not the conclusion—the logic is broken no matter how things end.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

illogical: Illogical means the steps of thinking go wrong — a conclusion that does not follow, a rule of sense broken along the way — and it can be entirely innocent. Fallacious adds a misleading edge: the flawed reasoning is dressed up to persuade, built well enough to take in a careless reader.

unsound: Unsound means resting on a defective foundation, whether the flaw sits in the facts or in the logic — a bridge design and an argument can both be unsound. Fallacious is the narrower verdict: the reasoning itself is broken, however true the individual facts may be.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sound: built on solid evidence and correct steps

valid: correctly reasoned, with conclusions that follow from the premises

Where it sits · how badly the reasoning breaks down — shaky → fallacious → incoherent

shaky vs. fallacious: A shaky argument has weak spots a good editor might shore up; a fallacious one is built on a genuine logical flaw and cannot stand as reasoned.

incoherent vs. fallacious: Incoherent lies beyond fallacious: a fallacious argument at least hangs together well enough to fool someone, while an incoherent one offers no recognizable chain of reasoning at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fallac

Root — fallac: deceiving (from Latin fallere, to deceive)

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by

Put it together

Put it together: Fallac- (deceiving) + -ious (full of) = full of deception. Latin fallere, 'to deceive or trip up,' also gives English fallacy and fault. A fallacious argument has deception built into its machinery—whether or not the speaker knows the gears are rigged.

Use the root in a new word: infallible

Use the root in a new word: infallible: No umpire is infallible; instant replay overturns a handful of calls every season.

Word Choice

formal / academic

Fallacious is a precision tool for arguments and reasoning—essays, editorials, proofs. Its neighbors in this unit split the work of 'false': spurious describes things and claims faked to look genuine, distortion names real facts twisted out of shape, and fallacious says the logic itself is broken. A wrong phone number is merely incorrect, never fallacious.
